title: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, CRANIOFACIAL ABNORMALITIES, AND SEIZURES
alt_titles: PSYCHOMOTOR RETARDATION, EPILEPSY, AND CRANIOFACIAL DYSMORPHISM

relationships.phenotype: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, CRANIOFACIAL ABNORMALITIES, AND SEIZURES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures (NEDHCS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SNIP1 gene (608241) on chromosome 1p34.3.

checks.claim: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures (NEDHCS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SNIP1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia due to a homozygous SNIP1 mutation.
checks.explanation: The paper links the disorder, which it calls symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia, to a homozygous SNIP1 mutation. NEDHCS is the OMIM name for the same disorder.

checks.claim: The SNIP1 gene is located on chromosome 1p34.3.
checks.evidence_quote: Symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia | 6 | 1 | rs2153337 | rs2225251 | 6.6 | 126
checks.explanation: The paper maps the locus to chromosome 1 only and does not give the 1p34.3 band. The band is standard gene-location nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are severe psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, seizures, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Puffenberger et al. (2012) described the disorder in Old Order Amish children.

checks.claim: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients were from Old Order Amish or Mennonite populations, received medical care at the Clinic for Special Children (CSC), and presented with a distinctive recessive clinical phenotype (Table 1).
checks.explanation: The paper describes all seven conditions, including this one, as recessive, and affected children are homozygous.

checks.claim: Severe psychomotor retardation is a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected children have severe psychomotor delay and do not learn to walk or speak.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Hypotonia is a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected neonates are hypotonic and feed poorly.
checks.explanation: Stated directly; the examination also shows hypotonia.

checks.claim: Seizures are a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: accompanied by focal or generalized seizures that can manifest as dystonic posturing, drop attacks, myoclonic jerks, or generalized tonic-clonic events. Multiple intractable seizure types can afflict an individual patient.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Craniofacial dysmorphism is a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: Dysmorphic features that evolve over time include a bulbous nose, wide mouth and tongue, broad jaw with protuberant angles, short hands, short tapered fingers, and broad thumbs
checks.explanation: Craniofacial dysmorphism and skull dysplasia are described.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) described neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures in Old Order Amish children.
checks.evidence_quote: An unlabeled probe melting analysis for this variant identified 5 carriers among 203 Old Order Amish controls (2.5%) (Table 4).
checks.explanation: Table 1 assigns the disorder to the Amish (A) group, and the controls screened were Old Order Amish.

paragraphs.text: Puffenberger et al. (2012) studied Old Order Amish children with severe psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, epilepsy, and craniofacial dysmorphism. They used genetic mapping and exome sequencing to study this disorder and several other new recessive disorders in Plain communities.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) studied Old Order Amish children with severe psychomotor retardation.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected children have severe psychomotor delay and do not learn to walk or speak.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The Old Order Amish children studied by Puffenberger et al. (2012) had hypotonia.
checks.evidence_quote: Examination typically reveals a subdued child with strabismus, slow horizontal nystagmus, hypotonia, and weak or absent tendon reflexes.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The Old Order Amish children studied by Puffenberger et al. (2012) had epilepsy.
checks.evidence_quote: Two affected brothers presented with severe psychomotor delay, intractable seizures, bulbous nose, wide mouth and tongue, broad jaw with protuberant angles
checks.explanation: The disorder is named symptomatic epilepsy, and patients have intractable seizures.

checks.claim: The Old Order Amish children studied by Puffenberger et al. (2012) had craniofacial dysmorphism.
checks.evidence_quote: Dysmorphic features that evolve over time include a bulbous nose, wide mouth and tongue, broad jaw with protuberant angles, short hands, short tapered fingers, and broad thumbs
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) used genetic mapping and exome sequencing to study this neurodevelopmental disorder and several other new recessive disorders in Plain communities.
checks.evidence_quote: Among the Plain people, we have used single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) microarrays to genetically map recessive disorders to large autozygous haplotype blocks
checks.explanation: The paper combines genetic mapping and exome sequencing for seven recessive disorders, six of them novel, in Plain communities.

paragraphs.text: Puffenberger et al. (2012) found homozygous SNIP1 mutations in affected children from Amish families, which is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) found homozygous SNIP1 mutations in affected children from Amish families.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome data on three affected individuals from two sibships revealed 34 homozygous variants in the mapped region. Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly)
checks.explanation: The affected Amish children from two sibships are homozygous.

checks.claim: The finding of homozygous SNIP1 mutations in affected Amish children is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients were from Old Order Amish or Mennonite populations, received medical care at the Clinic for Special Children (CSC), and presented with a distinctive recessive clinical phenotype (Table 1).
checks.explanation: Homozygosity in affected children fits the recessive model the paper describes.

paragraphs.text: In affected Old Order Amish children, Puffenberger et al. (2012) used homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing to identify a homozygous missense mutation in the SNIP1 gene (glu366-to-gly; E366G). For the disorders in their study, Puffenberger et al. (2012) stated that sibs and parents were also sequenced, when available, to confirm segregation of the allele within the family. They did not give segregation data specific to SNIP1.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) used homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing in affected Old Order Amish children.
checks.evidence_quote: Using between 1 and 5 patient samples per disorder, we identified sequence variants in the known disease-causing genes SLC6A3 and FLVCR1, and present evidence to strongly support the pathogenicity of variants identified in TUBGCP6, BRAT1, SNIP1, CRADD, and HARS.
checks.explanation: Autozygosity mapping followed by exome sequencing was used.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SNIP1 gene, E366G (glu366-to-gly), in affected Old Order Amish children.
checks.evidence_quote: Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly) (Table 3).
checks.explanation: A homozygous missense variant, p.Glu366Gly, matches E366G.

checks.claim: For the disorders in their study, Puffenberger et al. (2012) stated that sibs and parents were also sequenced, when available, to confirm segregation of the allele within the family.
checks.evidence_quote: In addition, siblings and parents were also sequenced, when available, to confirm appropriate segregation of the allele within the family.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) did not give segregation data specific to the SNIP1 mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome data on three affected individuals from two sibships revealed 34 homozygous variants in the mapped region. Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly) (Table 3).
checks.explanation: The SNIP1 sections give no family-specific segregation results; only the general statement covers this.

allelic_variants.name: SNIP1, GLU366GLY
allelic_variants.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures

paragraphs.text: In Old Order Amish children with psychomotor retardation, epilepsy, and craniofacial dysmorphism, Puffenberger et al. (2012) identified a homozygous c.1097A-G transition in the SNIP1 gene, resulting in a glu366-to-gly (E366G) substitution. The mutation was identified by exome sequencing combined with homozygosity mapping.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) identified a homozygous c.1097A-G transition in the SNIP1 gene in Old Order Amish children with psychomotor retardation, epilepsy, and craniofacial dysmorphism.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome data on three affected individuals from two sibships revealed 34 homozygous variants in the mapped region. Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly) (Table 3).
checks.explanation: c.1097A>G is an A-to-G transition, and the affected Amish children are homozygous.

checks.claim: The SNIP1 c.1097A-G transition results in a glu366-to-gly (E366G) substitution.
checks.explanation: Same variant in equivalent notation.

checks.claim: The SNIP1 c.1097A-G (E366G) mutation was identified by exome sequencing combined with homozygosity mapping.
checks.evidence_quote: For six disorders, an average autozygous block of 4.4 Mb (0.13% of the human genome) contained only one novel homozygous variant and rendered disease gene identification straightforward.
checks.explanation: The variant was found by exome sequencing within an autozygous mapped interval on chromosome 1.
